did_you_know.text: Did you know? Chapter 8 opens with a speech by Bildad the Shuhite, one of Job’s friends, who responds sharply to Job’s words.
Did you know? Bildad raises a fundamental question: Can God pervert justice or righteousness? In doing so, he defends the justice of God’s judgment.
Did you know? Bildad interprets the deaths of Job’s children as the result of their sin; in his view, God delivered them into the power of their wrongdoing.
Did you know? Bildad urges Job to seek God earnestly and plead with Him—that is, to turn to Him with a request and supplication.
Did you know? Bildad assures Job that if he is truly pure and upright, his future will be far greater than his beginning: “Your beginning will seem small, and your latter end will be very great.”
Did you know? Bildad directs Job to the generations of old and to the wisdom of the ancestors, so that he may learn from their experience and understanding.

Did you know? Bildad emphasizes the brevity of human life through the image of a shadow: people exist for only a short time and do not know everything, so they should listen to the wisdom of earlier generations.
Did you know? Bildad uses water plants—papyrus and reeds—to illustrate that anything that does not receive its source of nourishment cannot grow or survive.
Did you know? The confidence of the godless is compared to a spider’s web: a structure that appears to offer shelter but cannot serve as a firm support.

Did you know? At the end of his speech, Bildad declares that God does not reject the blameless or uphold evildoers; he promises joy to the righteous and foretells the shame of their enemies and the destruction of the wicked’s dwelling.
